## Story

> Kleeberg station post office, Friday night, ten past eleven. A power cut has wiped Iris, the machine that reads the handwritten postcodes on letters, and the night mail train leaves at 00:40. Ferdinand Kowalski, who built Iris, is on holiday; his apprentice Jonas tried to retrain her and gave up.
>
> Rebuild Iris's network, train it on her archive of digit cards, and sort the urgent letters before the train leaves. Python here runs a TensorFlow-style model: a small library with TensorFlow's names (`import tensorflow as tf`), written for this room because the real TensorFlow can't run in a browser. The first puzzle you open takes a little while to load.

## Stations

### 1. The envelope scanner

**Practises:** NumPy arrays as images: shapes, reshaping in the right order, splitting and stacking, scaling and inverting pixel values  
**Needs:** 🔎 The scanner's manual, 🔎 Iris's type plate  
**Data:** [scanner.py](../../content/rooms/nn-post/data/scanner.py)

**Task:**

> Before anything else, Iris has to see. The scanner by the door still works: a test envelope lies in it, and its output is loaded as `stream`, one long row of numbers.
>
> 1. Turn `stream` into the five digit images of the postcode: `digits`, with the shape `(5, 16, 16)`. The scanner's manual says how it reads an envelope.
> 2. Iris wants every pixel the way her type plate says. Convert `digits` to that.
> 3. Look at the digits with `show_images` and store the postcode as `postcode`, a string such as `"12345"`.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
import numpy as np
from helpers import show_images

print(stream.shape, stream.min(), stream.max())

digits = None     # shape (5, 16, 16), in Iris's format
postcode = None   # e.g. "12345"

# show_images(digits, labels=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
import numpy as np
from helpers import show_images

strip = stream.reshape(16, 80)              # the scanner reads 16 lines of 80 pixels
show_images(strip, title="Scanner strip")
digits = np.stack(np.hsplit(strip, 5))      # five boxes of 16 x 16
digits = 1 - digits / 255                   # Iris: ink 1.0, paper 0.0
show_images(digits, labels=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
postcode = "35781"
```

**Checked result** (`_scanner_check(digits, postcode)`):

```json
"read"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> The test envelope goes to **35781**, Kleeberg itself. Now you can read Ferdinand's sticker on the scanner too: "Scanner: 0 = ink, 255 = paper. Iris: ink 1.0, paper 0.0. Convert everything that comes out of here before Iris sees it!"

**Hints:**

1. `stream.reshape(5, 16, 16)` gives stripes, not digits: the scanner doesn't store one digit after the other. Reshape it to what it really reads first, and look at that with `show_images`.
2. The scanner reads 16 lines of 80 pixels: `strip = stream.reshape(16, 80)`. `np.hsplit(strip, 5)` cuts it into five 16 × 16 pieces, and `np.stack(...)` makes them one array. The scanner's 0 is black ink; Iris's ink is 1.0.
3. `digits = 1 - np.stack(np.hsplit(stream.reshape(16, 80), 5)) / 255`. The postcode is `"35781"`.

### 2. Iris's last backup

**Practises:** What a dense layer computes: matrix product, bias, ReLU, softmax; argmax as the prediction; the same network as Keras layers with set_weights  
**Needs:** open from the start  
**Data:** [wiring.py](../../content/rooms/nn-post/data/wiring.py)

**Task:**

> Ferdinand's old terminal still holds old Iris's network: `W1`, `b1`, `W2`, `b2`, and her six self-test cards, `cards`, already in her format. Every morning she read these cards and printed her reading on a slip.
>
> 1. Do by hand, with NumPy, what her network does. Each card as a row of 256 pixels, times `W1`, plus `b1`, then ReLU: `hidden`. Then times `W2`, plus `b2`, then softmax: `probs`, a row of 10 probabilities per card.
> 2. Her reading, `reading`: for each card the digit with the highest probability, as one string of six digits.
> 3. Rebuild old Iris as a Keras model, `old_iris`, with the same layers. Load her weights with `set_weights` and check that `old_iris.predict(cards)` gives your `probs`.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import layers
from helpers import show_images

show_images(cards, title="Self-test cards")
print(W1.shape, b1.shape, W2.shape, b2.shape)

hidden = None    # (6, 16): ReLU(cards as rows @ W1 + b1)
probs = None     # (6, 10): softmax(hidden @ W2 + b2)
reading = None   # e.g. "123456"

old_iris = None  # tf.keras.Sequential([...]) with old Iris's layers, then set_weights
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import layers
from helpers import show_images

show_images(cards, title="Self-test cards")
hidden = np.maximum(cards.reshape(6, 256) @ W1 + b1, 0)
scores = hidden @ W2 + b2
probs = np.exp(scores) / np.exp(scores).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
reading = "".join(str(d) for d in probs.argmax(axis=1))
print(reading, probs.max(axis=1).round(2))

old_iris = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.Input(shape=(16, 16)),
    layers.Flatten(),
    layers.Dense(16, activation="relu"),
    layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"),
])
old_iris.set_weights([W1, b1, W2, b2])
print(np.abs(old_iris.predict(cards) - probs).max())
```

**Checked result** (`_wiring_check(hidden, probs, reading, old_iris)`):

```json
"self-test passed"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> Old Iris reads **305118**. Look at the fourth card: it's a crossed 7, and she was sure it's a 1. With only 16 hidden neurons she learned too little.
>
> Your hand calculation and Keras agree: a Dense layer is a matrix product, a bias and an activation, nothing more.

**Hints:**

1. `cards.reshape(6, 256)` puts each card in one row. `@` multiplies matrices, and `np.maximum(x, 0)` is ReLU. Softmax: `np.exp(s)` divided by its sum in each row, `np.exp(s).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)`.
2. `probs.argmax(axis=1)` gives the digit for each card; `"".join(...)` makes a string. Old Iris in Keras: `Input(shape=(16, 16))`, `Flatten()`, `Dense(16, activation="relu")`, `Dense(10, activation="softmax")`; then `old_iris.set_weights([W1, b1, W2, b2])`.
3. `hidden = np.maximum(cards.reshape(6, 256) @ W1 + b1, 0)`, `scores = hidden @ W2 + b2`, `probs = np.exp(scores) / np.exp(scores).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)`. She reads `"305118"`, although the fourth card is a 7.

### 3. The blueprint

**Practises:** Sequential, Input, Flatten, Dense; counting parameters (inputs × neurons + one bias per neuron); summary()  
**Needs:** 🔎 Blueprint: Iris 2, 🔎 Iris's type plate  
**Data:** [blueprint.py](../../content/rooms/nn-post/data/blueprint.py)

**Task:**

> Ferdinand pinned three drafts for a new Iris to the wall. Only one of them fits on her memory chip.
>
> 1. Build the drafts as Keras models and let Keras count their parameters, with `summary()` or `count_params()`.
> 2. Store the draft that fits as `model`.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import layers

model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.Input(shape=(16, 16)),
    # ... the layers of a draft
])
model.summary()
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import layers

for first, second in [(128, 32), (64, 64), (64, 32)]:
    draft = tf.keras.Sequential([
        tf.keras.Input(shape=(16, 16)),
        layers.Flatten(),
        layers.Dense(first, activation="relu"),
        layers.Dense(second, activation="relu"),
        layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"),
    ])
    print(first, second, draft.count_params())

model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.Input(shape=(16, 16)),
    layers.Flatten(),
    layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
    layers.Dense(32, activation="relu"),
    layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"),
])
model.summary()
```

**Checked result** (`_blueprint_check(model)`):

```json
"fits"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> Draft C fits: **18,858** parameters, below the chip's 20,000. Its first layer alone has 256 × 64 + 64 = 16,448: in a dense network, most parameters sit where the pixels come in.

**Hints:**

1. Every draft starts with `layers.Flatten()`, which turns a 16 × 16 card into 256 numbers. A `Dense` layer has one weight per input and neuron, plus one bias per neuron. The type plate says how much the chip holds.
2. Draft A has 37,354 parameters and draft B 21,258. The chip holds 20,000.
3. Draft C: `tf.keras.Sequential([tf.keras.Input(shape=(16, 16)), layers.Flatten(), layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"), layers.Dense(32, activation="relu"), layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")])`.

**Model solution:**

```python
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import layers

tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(1)

model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.Input(shape=(16, 16)),
    layers.Flatten(),
    layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
    layers.Dense(32, activation="relu"),
    layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"),
])
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
history = model.fit(x_train / 255, y_train, epochs=10, validation_split=0.2)

test_loss, test_accuracy = model.evaluate(x_test / 255, y_test)
print("Test accuracy:", test_accuracy)
```

**Checked result** (`_apprentice_check(model)`):

```json
"in service"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> Iris 2 reads about **95 %** of the test cards. Jonas made three mistakes: a loss for one-hot labels with labels that are plain digits, ReLU on the output (all ten outputs can become 0, and the loss `nan`), and pixels from 0 to 255 instead of 0.0 to 1.0, which keeps the network from learning well.

**Hints:**

1. Read the error from the bottom: `target.shape=(None, 1), output.shape=(None, 10)`. The labels are single digits, not rows of ten 0s and 1s. Which loss takes labels like that? The handbook compares the two.
2. When the loss turns into `nan`, look at the last layer: Iris's output must be 10 probabilities that add up to 1. Then compare the archive label (how the cards are stored) with the type plate (what Iris expects).
3. `loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy"`, `activation="softmax"` in the last layer, and `x_train / 255` in `fit` and `x_test / 255` in `evaluate`.

**Model solution:**

```python
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from helpers import show_plot, replay

show_plot(log["loss"], log["val_loss"], labels=["loss", "val_loss"], title="Ferdinand's training run")
best_epoch = int(np.argmin(log["val_loss"])) + 1
stopper = tf.keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=3, restore_best_weights=True)
stop_epoch = replay(stopper, log)
kept_epoch = stopper.model.weights_from
print(best_epoch, stop_epoch, kept_epoch)
```

**Checked result** (`_logbook_check(best_epoch, stopper, stop_epoch, kept_epoch)`):

```json
"logged"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> The best epoch is **17**. After it the network learns the training cards by heart, and the validation loss climbs. With a patience of 3 the training survives the wobble at epochs 9 and 10, stops at epoch **20** and goes back to the weights of epoch 17. With a patience of 1 it would have stopped at epoch 9.

**Hints:**

1. The training loss keeps falling; the validation loss falls, wobbles, then rises again. `np.argmin(log["val_loss"])` is the position of its lowest value, counted from 0. The x axis of `show_plot` counts from 0 too.
2. Ferdinand's rules in Keras: `monitor="val_loss"`, `patience=3`, `restore_best_weights=True`. Then `stop_epoch = replay(stopper, log)`; it also prints which epoch's weights the model keeps.
3. `best_epoch = 17`, `stopper = tf.keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=3, restore_best_weights=True)`, `stop_epoch = 20`, `kept_epoch = 17`.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf

from helpers import show_images

tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(1)

model = None      # Iris 2

**Model solution:**

```python
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import layers
from helpers import show_images

tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(1)

model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.Input(shape=(16, 16)),
    layers.Flatten(),
    layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
    layers.Dense(32, activation="relu"),
    layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"),
])
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
stopper = tf.keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=3, restore_best_weights=True)
model.fit(x_train / 255, y_train, epochs=30, validation_split=0.2, callbacks=[stopper], verbose=2)
print(model.evaluate(x_test / 255, y_test))

letters = 1 - urgent.reshape(6, 16, 16) / 255
show_images(letters, title="Urgent letters")
bins = model.predict(letters).argmax(axis=1).tolist()
print(bins)
```

**Checked result** (`_sort_check(model, bins)`):

```json
"sorted"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> Iris's lens glows, the belt starts, and six letters drop into bins **4, 7, 1, 9, 2, 6**. At 00:39 the door of the mail car slides shut.
>
> One letter comes back the next morning: its sender wrote the digit in the corner of the box, not in the middle, and Iris read it wrong. A dense network learns which pixels light up where; move the digit, and it is lost. Networks that find shapes wherever they are come next: convolutional networks.

**Hints:**

1. Iris 2 is draft C, compiled and scaled as in Jonas's fixed script. Train with `validation_split=0.2` and Ferdinand's `EarlyStopping` in `callbacks=[...]`; `epochs=30` is fine, the stopper ends it in time.
2. The urgent letters come straight from the scanner, where 0 is ink. Reshape them to `(6, 16, 16)` and convert them as at the scanner; look at them with `show_images`. Then `model.predict(letters).argmax(axis=1)`.
3. `letters = 1 - urgent.reshape(6, 16, 16) / 255`. The bins are `[4, 7, 1, 9, 2, 6]`.

## Clues in the room

### 🔎 The scanner's manual

*Used by: 1. The envelope scanner*

> SCANNY 80 · postcode scanner
>
> Reads the postcode strip of an envelope: five boxes of 16 × 16 pixels side by side, so the strip is 16 pixels high and 80 wide.
>
> The scanner reads the strip like a page of text: line by line from the top, each line from left to right. It puts out one long row of numbers.
>
> Brightness: 0 = black, 255 = white.

### 🔎 Iris's type plate

*Used by: 1. The envelope scanner, 3. The blueprint, 4. Jonas's laptop*

> IRIS · automatic letter reader · Kleeberg station post office
>
> Input: one digit box of 16 × 16 pixels. Every pixel is a number from **0.0 (paper)** to **1.0 (ink)**.
>
> Output: 10 probabilities, one for each digit from 0 to 9. The highest wins.
>
> Memory chip: **20,000 numbers** (weights and biases).

### 🔎 Blueprint: Iris 2

*Used by: 3. The blueprint*

> IRIS 2 · drafts · F. Kowalski
>
> Every draft: input 16 × 16, then Flatten.
>
> Draft A: Dense 128 (ReLU) → Dense 32 (ReLU) → Dense 10 (softmax)
> Draft B: Dense 64 (ReLU) → Dense 64 (ReLU) → Dense 10 (softmax)
> Draft C: Dense 64 (ReLU) → Dense 32 (ReLU) → Dense 10 (softmax)
>
> In pencil: "Only one of them fits on the chip."

### 🔎 A note from Jonas

*Used by: 4. Jonas's laptop*

> Ferdinand, I tried to teach Iris 2 again, but the training crashes! The labels are digits, so categorical crossentropy must be right, no? I've gone home, sorry.
>
> Jonas
>
> P.S. The laptop password is the number of parameters of Iris 2.

### 🔎 The label on the archive boxes

*Used by: 4. Jonas's laptop*

> IRIS ARCHIVE · digit cards, sorted by hand
>
> 3,000 cards to learn from (`x_train`, `y_train`) and 600 to test with (`x_test`, `y_test`).
>
> Every card is 16 × 16 pixels, stored as bytes: **0 = paper, 255 = ink**. Labels: the digit on the card, 0 to 9.

### 🔎 Ferdinand's rules

*Used by: 5. Ferdinand's cabinet, 6. Iris*

> Rules for training Iris (F. K.)
>
> 1. Keep 20 % of the cards aside for validation.
> 2. Watch the validation loss, not the training loss.
> 3. Be patient: give her 3 epochs to get better before you stop.
> 4. Always go back to her best weights.
>
> Start code for Iris: the epoch the training stops at, then the epoch whose weights she keeps.

### 🔎 The departure board

*Used by: 6. Iris*

> NIGHT MAIL
>
> 00:40 · Post 2871 · Kleeberg → Hamburg · platform 1
>
> Urgent letters: Iris reads the first digit of the postcode (the postal zone, 0 to 9) and drops each letter into the bin with that number.

## Handbook in the room: 📖 Iris's service manual

**Images as arrays:** [`a.shape`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.ndarray.shape.html), [`a.reshape(rows, cols)`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.reshape.html), [`np.hsplit(a, n)  np.stack(arrays)`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.hsplit.html), [`1 - a / 255`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.broadcasting.html), `show_images(images, labels=None, title=None)`

**What a layer computes:** [`x @ W + b`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.matmul.html), [`ReLU: np.maximum(x, 0)`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/activations/relu), [`softmax`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/activations/softmax), [`a.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)  a.argmax(axis=1)`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.argmax.html)

**Building a model:** [`tf.keras.Sequential([...])`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/Sequential), [`layers.Flatten()`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/layers/Flatten), [`layers.Dense(units, activation=None)`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/layers/Dense), [`model.summary()  model.count_params()`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/Model#summary), [`model.set_weights([W1, b1, ...])`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/Model#set_weights)

**Training:** [`model.compile(optimizer, loss, metrics)`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/Model#compile), [`"sparse_categorical_crossentropy"`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/losses/SparseCategoricalCrossentropy), [`"categorical_crossentropy"`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/losses/CategoricalCrossentropy), [`model.fit(x, y, epochs, validation_split, callbacks)`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/Model#fit), [`history.history`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/callbacks/History), [`model.evaluate(x, y)  model.predict(x)`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/Model#predict), [`tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(n)`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/utils/set_random_seed)

**Stopping at the right time:** [`overfitting`](https://www.tensorflow.org/tutorials/keras/overfit_and_underfit), [`tf.keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor, patience, restore_best_weights)`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/callbacks/EarlyStopping), `replay(callback, history)`, `show_plot(*series, labels=None, title=None)`
